tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.
My sister's flat is larger than mine.
Of the three trails, this path is the worse.
The new bus stop is closer than the old one.
She sings more better than she did at the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Heavier" already marks the comparative, so "more heavier" doubles the form. Write "heavier" alone.

Tip: Drop "more" when the adjective already ends in -er.

TRUE — One-syllable "large" correctly takes -er: "larger than".

Tip: Short adjectives usually add -er, not "more."

FALSE — Ranking among three trails needs the superlative "worst," not the comparative "worse."

Tip: Of three or more → -est / worst / best; of two → -er / worse / better.

TRUE — One-syllable "close" correctly forms "closer than" for a two-item comparison.

Tip: Two things → comparative; a whole group → superlative.

FALSE — "Better" is already comparative; "more better" is a double mark. Use "better" alone.

Tip: Never stack "more" with an irregular comparative.
tasks.solution_overview: Scan each sentence for how comparison is marked. Watch for double forms (more + -er) and check whether you need a comparative (two items) or a superlative (a group). Irregulars like better/worse already carry the meaning — do not add "more."

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.
That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.
The evening train was quieter than the morning service.
This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.
It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Freshest" correctly ranks one bakery among five.

Tip: Use -est / most when ranking inside a group of three or more.

FALSE — The irregular comparative of "good" is "better," not "gooder."

Tip: Memorise good → better → best; never invent -er on irregulars.

TRUE — Two-syllable "quiet" correctly takes -er: "quieter."

Tip: Many short adjectives use -er / -est rather than more / most.

TRUE — Multi-syllable "interesting" correctly takes "more … than."

Tip: Longer adjectives prefer more/most, not -er/-est.

FALSE — "Coldest" is already a superlative; "most coldest" doubles it. Use "the coldest."

Tip: Never pair "most" with an -est form.
tasks.solution_overview: Check whether the adjective needs -er/-est or more/most, and whether any irregular (good/better/best) is mangled. Double superlatives like "most coldest" are always wrong.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is more taller than his twin brother.
Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.
Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.
The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.
My laptop runs gooder after the software update.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Taller" already includes the comparative; delete "more."

Tip: more + -er is never needed.

FALSE — Ranking among all desserts needs "the least sweet," not "the less sweet."

Tip: less = comparative (two); least = superlative (a group).

TRUE — Two-syllable "clear" commonly takes -er: "clearer than."

Tip: Many clear-type adjectives accept -er as well as more.

FALSE — "Worse" is already comparative; "more worser" piles two errors. Use "worse."

Tip: bad → worse → worst; never add more or -er.

FALSE — Replace "gooder" with "better."

Tip: good / better / best is fixed — no homemade forms.
tasks.solution_overview: This set stacks the beginner traps: double marking, less vs least, and broken irregulars. Fix the comparison word first, then check whether the sentence compares two things or ranks a whole set.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.
She chose the most cheap ticket available online.
Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.
This playlist is the best of the three we built.
The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Easy" correctly becomes "easier" (y → i + -er).

Tip: Consonant + y adjectives change y to i before -er/-est.

FALSE — One-syllable "cheap" takes "cheapest," not "most cheap."

Tip: Prefer -est on short adjectives unless the form sounds awkward.

TRUE — "Smaller than" is the standard comparative for "small."

Tip: Double the final consonant when needed (big → bigger), but "small" simply adds -er.

TRUE — "The best of the three" correctly uses the irregular superlative for a set of three.

Tip: good → better → best.

FALSE — "Farther/further" is already comparative; do not add "more." Use "farther/further … than."

Tip: Irregulars never take an extra "more."
tasks.solution_overview: Confirm spelling of -er forms, avoid "most" on short adjectives that want -est, and leave irregulars like best and farther alone — they do not need "more."

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.
Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.
She felt worse after skipping breakfast.
Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.
His second attempt was better than the first.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Spicy" correctly forms "spicier" for a two-item food comparison.

Tip: -y adjectives → -ier / -iest.

FALSE — With only two coats, use the comparative "warmer," not the superlative "warmest."

Tip: Between two → comparative; among many → superlative.

TRUE — "Worse" is the correct irregular comparative of "bad/ill."

Tip: bad/ill → worse → worst.

FALSE — Ranking four rooms needs "the quietest" (or "the most quiet"), not "the more quiet."

Tip: Superlative for a group of three or more.

TRUE — "Better than" correctly compares two attempts.

Tip: Two items → better; a whole group → best.
tasks.solution_overview: Focus on the two-versus-many rule. "Between the two" almost always wants a comparative, while "of the four" wants a superlative. Keep irregular worse/better clean.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.
This café is more popular than the one by the river.
My phone battery lasts longer than yours.
She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.
He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Tidy" correctly becomes "tidier" after a clear-up.

Tip: consonant + y → -ier.

TRUE — Multi-syllable "popular" correctly takes "more … than."

Tip: Three-syllable adjectives almost always use more/most.

TRUE — "Longer than" correctly compares battery life for two phones.

Tip: Duration often uses long / longer / longest.

TRUE — "The least expensive" correctly ranks cost among many bikes.

Tip: least + adjective = superlative of inferiority.

FALSE — "Faster" already marks the comparative; delete "more."

Tip: Adverbs formed with -er also reject an extra "more."
tasks.solution_overview: Most sentences here are clean models. The one clear fault is stacking "more" on an -er adverb. Treat least + adjective as the standard way to rank "smallest amount of" a quality.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The river is deeper here than near the bridge.
Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.
Their dog is friendlier than ours.
She felt more happier after the phone call.
This is the worst film I have seen all year.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Deeper than" correctly compares two stretches of the river.

Tip: One-syllable adjectives take -er for two-item contrasts.

FALSE — Only two recipes → use "simpler," not the superlative "the simplest."

Tip: Of/between two → comparative.

TRUE — "Friendly" correctly forms "friendlier" ("more friendly" is also acceptable).

Tip: -y adjectives commonly take -ier.

FALSE — "Happier" already includes the comparative; remove "more."

Tip: happy → happier → happiest.

TRUE — "The worst" is the correct irregular superlative.

Tip: bad → worse → worst.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch "of the two" — that phrase almost always blocks a superlative. Keep -ier spelling tidy and leave irregular worst alone.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.
He is the elder of the two cousins.
This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.
Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.
We walked further than planned before turning back.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Less exciting than" correctly compares two episodes with a longer adjective.

Tip: less + adjective + than = comparative of inferiority.

TRUE — "Elder" is a traditional comparative used for people in a family pair; "the elder of the two" is fine.

Tip: elder/eldest mainly for family; older/oldest for general age.

FALSE — Spelling and form fail: write "bigger than," not "bigest than."

Tip: big → bigger → biggest (double g); and use comparative with than.

TRUE — "The most relaxing" correctly ranks one hobby among several.

Tip: -ing adjectives of three syllables take most.

TRUE — "Further than" is a standard irregular comparative of distance/extent.

Tip: farther/further both work for physical distance in modern English.
tasks.solution_overview: This set adds less + adjective, family elder, and the spelling trap big → bigger. Read than-clauses carefully: they want a comparative, not a mangled superlative spelling.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.
Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.
The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.
He is not as tall as his older sister.
The sequel was as good than the original.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Equality uses "as + adjective + as."

Tip: as … as compares sameness, not ranking.

FALSE — After "as neat" you need "as," not "than": "as neat as."

Tip: than belongs with comparatives; as … as marks equality.

TRUE — "As peaceful as" correctly states equal calm.

Tip: Keep both as-markers; dropping the second one breaks the pattern.

TRUE — "Not as tall as" is the standard negative equality pattern.

Tip: not as … as ≈ less … than in everyday meaning.

FALSE — Replace "than" with "as": "as good as the original."

Tip: Never mix as … than.
tasks.solution_overview: Equality comparisons live in the as … as frame. If you see than after as + adjective, the sentence is wrong — swap than for the second as.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She drives much more carefully than she did last year.
This bag is far heavier than it looks.
The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.
He speaks English better than I expected.
They arrived slightly earlier than the others.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Intensifier "much" correctly strengthens "more carefully."

Tip: much / far / a lot can boost comparatives.

TRUE — "Far heavier" correctly intensifies a short comparative.

Tip: far + -er is natural and strong.

FALSE — "A lot more harder" doubles the comparative. Use "a lot harder" or "much harder."

Tip: Intensifiers sit before one comparative form, not two.

TRUE — "Better than" correctly compares performance; "I expected" is a fine clause after than.

Tip: Irregular better needs no "more."

TRUE — "Slightly earlier" correctly softens the comparative of "early."

Tip: slightly / a bit / rather can modify comparatives.
tasks.solution_overview: Intensifiers (much, far, a lot, slightly) are fine before a single comparative. They become wrong the moment they sit beside a second comparative marker such as more + -er.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.
She is one of the smarter students in the class.
This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.
He is one of the tallest player on the team.
That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "One of the most + adjective + plural noun" is the correct pattern.

Tip: one of the + superlative + plural.

FALSE — After "one of the" you need a superlative: "one of the smartest students."

Tip: one of the blocks ordinary comparatives.

TRUE — "One of the best meals" correctly pairs irregular superlative with plural.

Tip: best / worst fit the same frame.

FALSE — "One of" requires a plural noun: "one of the tallest players."

Tip: one of + plural always.

FALSE — Use the superlative: "one of the funniest jokes."

Tip: Comparative -er forms do not follow "one of the."
highlights: one of the most beautiful cities
tasks.solution_overview: Remember the fixed frame: one of the + superlative + plural noun. Comparatives and singular nouns after "one of" are the usual exam traps.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The more she practised, the more confident she became.
The harder he trained, the better his times got.
More she waited, more anxious she felt.
The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.
The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "The more …, the more …" correctly links two parallel comparatives.

Tip: Keep "the" before each comparative in this pattern.

TRUE — Mixed forms work: "the harder …, the better …"

Tip: -er and irregular comparatives both fit the frame.

FALSE — Restore the articles: "The more she waited, the more anxious she felt."

Tip: Dropping "the" breaks the correlative comparative.

TRUE — "The less …, the happier …" is a valid inferiority pair.

Tip: less / fewer can lead the first half.

TRUE — "The sooner …, the cheaper …" is a classic fixed double comparative.

Tip: Time and cost often appear in this pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: Correlative comparatives need "the + comparative" in both halves. If either "the" disappears, rebuild the sentence before you mark it true.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.
He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.
Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.
The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.
They danced more graceful than the other couple.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "More skilfully" correctly forms the comparative of a -ly adverb.

Tip: Long adverbs take more/most, not -er.

TRUE — "Quicker" (or "more quickly") is acceptable in modern usage for manner here.

Tip: Short adverb comparatives often allow -er in everyday English.

FALSE — Use "more slowly," not "more slow," when modifying the verb speak.

Tip: Adjective slow ≠ adverb slowly.

TRUE — "Better" correctly compares how they sang on two occasions.

Tip: well → better → best (adverb).

FALSE — Manner needs "more gracefully," not the adjective "graceful."

Tip: After danced/spoke/sang, prefer adverb forms.
tasks.solution_overview: Separate adjective and adverb comparison. When the word modifies a verb (speak, dance, sing), you usually need an adverb comparative — more slowly / more gracefully / better — not a bare adjective.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.
Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.
Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.
The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.
His answer was different from mine.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Latinate "superior" pairs with "to," not "than": "superior to."

Tip: superior / inferior / preferable → to.

TRUE — "Inferior to" is the correct fixed comparative-like pattern.

Tip: Do not rewrite these with -er forms.

TRUE — "Preferable to" correctly states a preference between two options.

Tip: preferable to = better as a choice than.

FALSE — Replace "than" with "to": "preferable to the inland route."

Tip: Preferable never takes than.

TRUE — "Different from" is the standard British exam form.

Tip: Treat different from as safe in exams.
tasks.solution_overview: Some comparison words never take than. Superior, inferior, and preferable lock to "to." Learn those fixed prepositions separately from ordinary -er / more patterns.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.
We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.
She made less mistakes on the second draft.
He drinks less coffee than he used to.
There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Fewer people" correctly uses fewer with a countable plural.

Tip: fewer + countable; less + uncountable.

TRUE — "Less time" correctly pairs with uncountable time.

Tip: time, money, traffic, and advice usually take less.

FALSE — "Mistakes" is countable; write "fewer mistakes."

Tip: If you can count them, prefer fewer in careful English.

TRUE — "Less coffee" correctly treats coffee as an uncountable amount.

Tip: less + mass noun.

FALSE — "Traffic" is uncountable; use "less traffic," not "fewer traffic."

Tip: fewer needs a plural countable noun.
tasks.solution_overview: Less and fewer are comparative quantity words. Decide first whether the noun is countable plural or an uncountable mass, then pick fewer or less.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.
The music grew more and more louder near the stage.
The waves became higher and higher before the storm.
She felt worse and worse during the long flight.
The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Busier and busier" correctly shows gradual increase with a repeated comparative.

Tip: Adj-er and adj-er = steadily more.

FALSE — "More and more louder" doubles the marking. Use "louder and louder" or "more and more loud."

Tip: Pick one comparative system and stick to it.

TRUE — "Higher and higher" correctly intensifies a short comparative.

Tip: Repeat the -er form for gradual change.

TRUE — "Worse and worse" correctly repeats the irregular comparative.

Tip: Irregulars can double the same way: better and better, worse and worse.

FALSE — "Increasingly" already means "more and more," so "increasingly more difficult" is redundant. Prefer "increasingly difficult" or "more and more difficult."

Tip: Do not stack increasingly with more.
tasks.solution_overview: Gradual-change patterns either repeat one comparative (louder and louder) or use more and more + base adjective. Mixing systems — or adding increasingly to more — creates double marking.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.
This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.
She is taller than any girl in her class.
This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.
He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "No other … as … as" correctly sets up a unique equality comparison.

Tip: no other + as … as ≈ this is the cleanest.

TRUE — "Cheaper than any other" correctly excludes the rest of the set.

Tip: any other keeps the compared item outside the group.

FALSE — Include herself out of the group: "taller than any other girl" (or "anyone else").

Tip: Without other/else, the sentence oddly includes her in "any girl."

FALSE — Do not mix "the shortest" with "of any other." Prefer "the shortest path" or "shorter than any other path."

Tip: Superlative and "any other" usually fight each other.

TRUE — "Better than anyone else" correctly uses else to exclude him.

Tip: else / other prevents logical self-comparison.
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced comparison often hinges on exclusion words: other and else. Without them, a person can be compared with a group that still includes that person — a classic logic trap.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.
She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.
They would rather stay in than go out tonight.
He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.
We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Prefer A to B" is the standard comparative preference pattern.

Tip: prefer + noun/gerund + to + noun/gerund.

FALSE — Prefer takes "to," not "than": "prefers tea to coffee."

Tip: prefer … than is almost always wrong.

TRUE — "Would rather … than …" correctly contrasts two base-verb options.

Tip: would rather + bare infinitive + than + bare infinitive.

FALSE — After "would rather" use the bare infinitive: "would rather leave," not "would rather to leave."

Tip: Delete to after would rather.

TRUE — "Prefer … rather than …" is an accepted alternative to prefer … to … with parallel -ing forms.

Tip: Keep the two sides parallel (cooking / ordering).
tasks.solution_overview: Preference structures are cousins of comparatives: prefer A to B, and would rather A than B. Watch the preposition (to, not than) and the bare infinitive after would rather.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.
This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.
Her second cake was twice as large as the first.
The second half was half as long than the opening act.
Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Nowhere near as … as" correctly intensifies a negative equality comparison.

Tip: nowhere near as / not nearly as + adjective + as.

FALSE — Keep the as … as frame: "not nearly as steep as …," not "than."

Tip: Intensifiers do not change the need for a second as.

TRUE — "Twice as large as" correctly multiplies an equality comparison.

Tip: twice / three times + as + adjective + as.

FALSE — Write "half as long as," not "half as long than."

Tip: Multipliers still need as … as.

TRUE — "Slightly less humid than" correctly softens a comparative of inferiority.

Tip: less + adjective + than remains available beside as … as patterns.
tasks.solution_overview: Scaled equality (twice as, half as, not nearly as, nowhere near as) still needs a closing as. Than only returns when you switch to a true comparative such as less … than.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.
She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.
This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.
He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.
That was by far a better concert than the one in March.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Of all … the freshest" correctly pairs a group phrase with a superlative.

Tip: of all / among all → superlative.

TRUE — "By far the most organised" correctly intensifies a superlative.

Tip: by far / easily / much the + superlative.

FALSE — With "much the," use a superlative: "much the hardest," not "much the harder."

Tip: much the + -est / most …

TRUE — "Easily the funniest" correctly strengthens a superlative ranking.

Tip: easily the + superlative is common in speech and exams.

TRUE — "By far a better … than" can intensify a comparative when two concerts are compared.

Tip: by far works with both superlatives and clear two-item comparatives.
tasks.solution_overview: Final polish: intensifiers like by far, easily, and much the usually lock onto superlatives. If the sentence clearly compares only two items, a comparative after by far can still work — but "much the harder" is the wrong grade of comparison.
